assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks combine magic-wavelength trapping with ultranarrow optical transitions, giving fractional uncertainties at or below 1e-18 and turning time into the most precise measurement we have. This is exactly the kind of advance in 'what we can measure, and how accurately' that I value as an atomic physicist. The idea is original, the result is clean, and the impact reaches metrology, geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and the planned redefinition of the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated early Sr clocks; Ye's JILA group pushed the stability and accuracy and the many-body and spectroscopic control. The two-name configuration is natural. Credit from the broader trapped-ion clock and frequency-comb lines is already recognised by earlier prizes (as I recall them), and I have not verified every detail.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently confirmed by many groups worldwide, with international clock comparisons and stable interpretation. Recognition is timely; the redefinition of the second is still pending, but the science is settled.
uncertainties: Some credit, for example to Sr-lattice work by others such as Takamoto or to Ye's frequency-comb and Sr-clock collaborators, falls outside the supplied names.
Whether the committee would prefer to bundle the clocks with ultracold molecules or comb physics in a larger configuration.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation of Hubbard-type models with ultracold atoms in optical lattices opened a controllable, tunable platform for strongly correlated matter, from the superfluid to Mott insulator transition to single-site quantum gas microscopes. The conceptual proposal and the experimental realisation together are original and clearly foundational for modern quantum simulation, bridging atomic physics and condensed matter.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and others) supplied the theoretical proposal and Bloch and Greiner the decisive experiments, including the Mott transition and later microscopy. Cirac is also credited and contributed strongly to quantum simulation theory, but only three names fit; I choose the proposal-plus-experiment combination. Names such as Jaksch or Hänsch are not on the supplied list, which leaves an attribution gap.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature: replicated across many laboratories, with quantum gas microscopes and extended Hubbard physics widely adopted. Timely, though the physics of hard Hubbard regimes such as d-wave pairing is still open, which does not prevent recognition of the platform.
uncertainties: Allocation between Zoller and Cirac is a tension, and the contributions of Jaksch and Hänsch are not on the list.
Whether the prize should rest on the lattice-simulation platform or leave it to a broader quantum-simulation award.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry uses matter-wave coherence for precision measurement of gravity, rotation and fundamental constants, and now underlies gravimeters, gyroscopes and tests of the equivalence principle. Strong originality and clear measurement impact, and conceptually close to the laser spectroscopy and coherent control I know well.
assessment.attribution: Bordé developed the theory and the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer, Pritchard demonstrated early atom-optics and interferometers, and Kasevich pushed precision gravimetry and large-momentum-transfer techniques. Others such as Chu (already a laureate for cooling) and Mlynek, Keith and Rasel also contributed, so decisive credit is spread and the selection of three is not obvious.
assessment.maturity: Mature in laboratory and increasingly in field instruments; interpretation is stable. Recognition is reasonable, though the largest payoffs such as space-based tests and gravitational-wave detection are still prospective.
uncertainties: Several comparable contributors, including earlier laureates' work, make fair attribution difficult.
I am relying on memory for the priority of the early interferometer demonstrations.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics created the architecture used for superconducting qubit readout and coupling, bringing strong light-matter coupling into a solid-state circuit. It is original, widely used and the working basis of leading quantum processors.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and collaborators proposed it in 2004 and Wallraff with Schoelkopf demonstrated strong coupling. Blais is credited with the theory but cannot be included in a three-person prize alongside the experimental trio; I favour Girvin for theory and Wallraff and Schoelkopf for experiment. This is a close call.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed across many groups, and the interpretation is stable. A recent prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits (as I recall), so timing relative to that award deserves care.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as sufficiently distinct from the earlier superconducting-circuit prize.
Blais is left out of the proposed configuration.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade and programmable neutral-atom arrays provide a route to quantum gates, many-body simulation and quantum computing with individually trapped atoms. Strong scientific importance and clear relevance to atomic-physics tools I know, including coherent control and optical addressing.
assessment.attribution: Lukin and collaborators proposed the Rydberg-blockade scheme for gates and ensemble, Saffman contributed the gate proposals and demonstrations, and Browaeys with Grangier demonstrated blockade and tweezers arrays. Four names are credited and only three can be selected, so Grangier or Jaksch-type contributions are excluded.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly growing and replicated, but the field is still maturing: logical-qubit performance and scalability are not yet settled. Possibly somewhat premature for a prize now.
uncertainties: Premature if the field's long-term impact is judged by fault-tolerant computation.
Credit among Lukin, Saffman, Browaeys and Grangier is contested in the community; I cannot verify the priority sequence.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond gave a room-temperature solid-state spin system usable for quantum sensing, nanoscale magnetometry and bioimaging. This fits my interest in coherent light-matter interactions in crystals and in sensing.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko provided the single-centre optical detection and spin readout, and Lukin's group advanced coherent control, sensing and the quantum register concept. The assignment seems plausible, but the contribution of others such as Awschalom, Hanson and Hollenberg is not on the supplied list.
assessment.maturity: Mature in the lab, with a large user community; applications in biology and materials are still developing. Timing seems reasonable though not pressing.
uncertainties: Several other leading groups may have a claim to priority or equal contribution.
Practical impact in sensing is still maturing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Titanium-sapphire gain media and passive mode-locking (Kerr-lens and semiconductor saturable absorber mirrors) made reliable femtosecond lasers a standard laboratory tool, underlying frequency combs, ultrafast spectroscopy and attosecond science. High lasting impact, and as a laser spectroscopist I know the practical importance well.
assessment.attribution: Moulton developed the Ti:sapphire laser, Sibbett's group discovered Kerr-lens mode-locking and Keller developed SESAMs and ultrafast diode-pumped lasers. This is a reasonably clean three-way split, though the Kerr-lens discovery involved others as I recall.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature and widely adopted. Earlier prizes recognised chirped-pulse amplification, femtochemistry and the frequency comb, which touches the same technology, so novelty relative to those awards is a concern.
uncertainties: The precise attribution of Kerr-lens mode-locking is uncertain to me.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Direct laser cooling and magneto-optical trapping of molecules extended laser-cooling methods to molecules, opening precision tests such as the electron electric dipole moment and ultracold chemistry and quantum simulation with molecules. It is an original extension of work that was already recognised for atoms.
assessment.attribution: DeMille, Doyle and Tarbutt each led decisive experiments on molecular laser cooling and trapping; the three-name credit looks fair. Other groups, including those producing ultracold molecules from atoms, fall in a separate candidate.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently by several groups, but the field is still developing and the main scientific payoffs, such as improved EDM limits and quantum computing with molecules, are not yet fully realised, so it may be slightly premature.
uncertainties: The relation to the separate ultracold-molecule candidate is unclear.
Premature if the main impact lies in future applications.
